extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students of humor, comedians and comedy writers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria for creating or recognizing anti-humor (anti-comedy) — jokes that rely on omission, anticlimax, or reversal of expectations rather than a conventional punchline. Useful for comedians, writers, or analysts studying alternative comedy forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise from absence of expected joke/punch line
rubrics_metrics.description: Anti-humor ... is a type of alternative humor that is based on the surprise factor of absence of an expected joke or of a punch line in a narration that is set up as a joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up the narration like a conventional joke to create expectation, then withhold the expected punchline; the absence itself should generate the surprise that can produce a humorous effect for some audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticlimax (shaggy dog / the yarn)
rubrics_metrics.description: The yarn, also called a shaggy dog story, is a type of anti-humor that involves telling an extremely long joke with an intricate (and sometimes grisly) back story and surreal or repetitive plotline, before ending the story with either a weak spoonerism, or abruptly stopping with no real punchline at all, or no soap radio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use extended, elaborate, or repetitive narrative detail to build expectation; conclude with a deliberately weak, trivial, or absent payoff (e.g., an underwhelming spoonerism or an abrupt non-punchline) so the anticlimax becomes the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious punchline (the punchline is the most obvious element)
rubrics_metrics.description: The obvious punchline involves narratives that are structured like a traditional joke including a set-up and punchline, but whose punchline is the most obvious to the narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the 'punchline' be a literal, unsurprising, or perfectly logical answer so that the expected clever twist is replaced by banality; examples include 'Why did the chicken cross the road?' and farmer-joke variants where the reply is simply the literal answer ('Where's my tractor?').

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional reversal: provoke non-humorous reactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Anti-humor is described as a form of irony or reversal of expectations that may provoke an emotion opposite to humor, such as fear, pain, embarrassment, disgust, awkwardness, or discomfort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design material so the reversal of expectation elicits emotions other than laughter — awkwardness, discomfort, or even disgust — as part of the comic effect. Recognize that this will polarize audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody of traditional joke structure / alternative comedy approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternative comedy, among its other aspects, parodies the traditional idea of the joke as a form of humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat anti-humor as a deliberate subversion of established joke mechanics (set-up/punchline); use parody and inversion to critique or lampoon conventional comedy forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberately 'bad' performance and persona techniques in stand-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Anti-humor jokes are also often associated with deliberately bad stand-up comedians. Andy Kaufman had his own unique brand of anti-humor, quasi-surrealist acts coupled with performance art; one of his best-known manifestations of this was his act as the fictional persona of Tony Clifton, an untalented lounge lizard entertainer. Norm Macdonald was another comedian sometimes associated with performing anti-humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In performance, adopt anti-performance tactics (playing an untalented persona, using surreal or performance-art elements, delivering intentionally awkward material) to produce discomfort or confusion as part of the act. Be aware performers may resist or debate the 'anti-humor' label.
